events.title: Tailwind CSS first released
events.summary: Adam Wathan published Tailwind CSS v0.1.0 on November 1, 2017 — a utility-first CSS framework built on PostCSS.
events.about: Tailwind shipped hundreds of single-purpose classes (`flex`, `mt-4`, `text-gray-700`) instead of pre-built components — developers composed designs in markup. It started as a side project and grew into a commercial ecosystem with Tailwind UI, Headless UI, and Catalyst.

narrative.whyChosen: Tailwind introduced utility-first CSS as a credible alternative to Bootstrap components.
narrative.whyImportant: It changed how front-end teams think about styling — composition over custom CSS files.
narrative.problemSolved: Component frameworks forced designs into predefined patterns; custom CSS did not scale across teams.

events.title: iPhone X released
events.summary: Apple began selling the iPhone X on November 3, 2017 — Face ID, an edge-to-edge OLED display, and the notch.
events.about: The X eliminated the home button and introduced safe areas — every iOS app had to adapt layouts for the notch and gesture navigation. Face ID APIs replaced Touch ID for secure auth in a generation of flagship apps.

narrative.whyChosen: The iPhone X redefined iOS layout with the notch, gestures, and Face ID.
narrative.whyImportant: Safe-area insets and facial authentication became mandatory considerations for iOS developers.
narrative.problemSolved: Bezels and home buttons dominated phone design; secure face unlock was not mainstream.

events.title: Firefox 57 Quantum released
events.summary: Mozilla shipped Firefox 57 on November 14, 2017 — branded Firefox Quantum with a new CSS engine (Stylo), Rust components, and multi-process tabs.
events.about: Quantum was Firefox's fight back against Chrome: Servo's parallel styling code merged into Gecko, Rust replaced C++ in hot paths, and Project Quantum made the browser feel fast again. It proved Mozilla could still compete on performance with an independent engine.

narrative.whyChosen: Firefox Quantum was the biggest Firefox rewrite since tabbed browsing.
narrative.whyImportant: It kept Gecko alive as a credible alternative to Blink with measurable speed gains.
narrative.problemSolved: Firefox had fallen behind Chrome on speed and memory use, losing users and developer mindshare.

events.title: Sanity launched
events.summary: Sanity went live on November 14, 2017 — opening its API-first headless CMS and customizable React-based Studio to the public.
events.about: Sanity stores structured content in a real-time Content Lake queried via GROQ — developers define schemas in code and customize the editing UI in React. It competed with Contentful and Strapi as teams adopted JAMstack and decoupled frontends.

narrative.whyChosen: Sanity brought real-time structured content and a customizable open-source Studio.
narrative.whyImportant: GROQ and Portable Text set patterns for developer-centric headless CMS design.
narrative.problemSolved: Headless CMSs offered APIs but locked teams into rigid, uncustomizable admin UIs.

events.title: Symfony 4.0 released
events.summary: Symfony 4.0 shipped on November 30, 2017 — embracing PHP 7.1+, autowiring, and a micro-kernel for smaller apps.
events.about: Symfony 4 made dependency injection automatic and shrunk the framework footprint — `symfony/skeleton` became the starting point for APIs and microservices. Flex composer plugin streamlined installs; the release kept Symfony central to Laravel components and Drupal.

narrative.whyChosen: Symfony 4's autowiring and Flex modernized PHP framework bootstrapping.
narrative.whyImportant: Smaller kernels and autowired services matched the microservice era.
narrative.problemSolved: Symfony 3 required verbose service configuration for everyday dependency injection.
